text: SAFER Alameda Act — Preparing Alameda for Sea- Level Rise, Accidents, Flooding, Earthquakes, Resilience. To prepare for emergencies, earthquakes and sea-level rise; prevent flooded Tubes; repair potholes; keep streets safe and accessible; maintain response to fires, accidents, and medical emergencies; prevent Bay pollution; and protect shorelines; shall the City of Alameda measure issuing $300,000,000 in bonds, levying $49/$100,000 of assessed value, generating approximately $19,000,000 annually while bonds are outstanding, requiring oversight, public disclosures, and local control, be adopted?

This measure was placed on the ballot by the City Council of the City of Alameda. The measure would authorize the City to issue $300,000,000 in general obligation bonds to fund certain capital improvement projects in the City. If the voters approve the measure, the issued bonds would be repaid through an ad valorem property tax levied on taxable property in the City. It is anticipated that property owners will be annually assessed an average of $49 per $100,000 of assessed value of their property for this purpose. A property’s assessed value is annually determined by the County Assessor and is not the same as the property’s fair market value.
The measure requires fiscal accountability, including a City Council-appointed oversight committee that will have responsibility for reviewing and reporting on the expenditure of the bond proceeds.
The measure provides that bond proceeds will be used for capital improvement projects falling into the following general categories:
Preventing Flooding and Combating Sea-Level Rise. Project examples include:
Levees, sea walls, flood walls, ecosystem restoration and nature-based solutions to mitigate shoreline flooding from sea level rise
Stormwater detention basins to expand stormwater storage capacity
Replacing storm drain pipes and culverts, and drainage improvements to reduce surface flooding

Storm pump station upgrades
Preparing for Earthquakes and Emergencies. Project examples include:
Fire Stations 1, 2 and 4 earthquake retrofits and other safety-related improvements

Structural improvements to the Alameda Police Department and improvements to optimize the use of the existing facility, including construction of an evidence storage room
Maintaining Responses to Fires, Accidents, and Medical Emergencies.
Project examples include:
Constructing a new fire station on the west side of Alameda, including relocating and consolidating at the new station Fire Administration, Fire Prevention, and emergency medical services.

Relocating and building a Fleet Services Maintenance Facility that would include infrastructure for charging the City’s electrical vehicles Repairing Potholes and Keeping Streets Safe and Accessible. Project examples include:
Paving streets and repairing potholes
Sidewalk and park ADA improvements
Traffic signal upgrades to improve traffic flow and limit congestion

Street safety improvements to reduce accidents and improve traffic flow at intersections
Keeping Pollution Out of the Bay.
Project examples include:

Storm system upgrades that may include trash capture, pollution control, green infrastructure and other related improvements
A “Yes” vote is a vote to allow the City to issue general obligation bonds in the amount of $300,000,000 to fund certain capital improvement projects. A “No” vote is a vote not to allow the issuance of general obligation bonds in any amount.
Passage of this Measure requires a “Yes” vote by two-thirds of the voters who vote on the measure.
Tax Rate Statement Of Bond Measure L

An election will be held in the City of Alameda (the “City”) on November 3, 2026 to authorize the sale of up to $300,000,000 in general obligation bonds of the City to finance the municipal improvements listed in the bond measure. If such bonds are authorized, the City expects to sell the bonds in one or more series. Principal and interest on the bonds will be payable solely from the proceeds of ad valorem tax levies made upon the taxable property in the City. The following information is provided in compliance with applicable provisions of the California Elections Code. Such information contains the best estimates from official sources, based on assessed valuations available at the time of the filing of this statement, projections based on experience within the City and other demonstrable factors. Based upon the foregoing:
1. The best estimate of the average annual tax rate that would be required to be levied to fund the bond issue over the entire duration of the bond debt service, is $0.04797 per $100 (or $47.97 per $100,000) of assessed valuation of all property to be taxed. The best estimate of the final fiscal year in which the tax is anticipated to be collected is 2061. 2. The best estimate of the highest tax rate that would be required to be levied to fund the bond issue, based on assessed valuations available at the time of filing this statement is $0.04949 per $100 (or $49.49 per $100,000) of assessed valuation of all property to be taxed. The best estimate of the first fiscal year in which the highest tax rate will apply is 2028.
3. The best estimate of the total debt service, including the principal and interest, that would be required to be repaid if all the bonds are issued and sold is $662,197,756. Voters should note that such estimated tax rates are specific to the repayment of bonds issued under this authorization and are and will be in addition to tax rates levied in connection with other bond authorizations approved or to be approved by the voters of the City or any other overlapping public agency.
Voters should note that estimated tax rate is based on the ASSESSED VALUE of taxable property within the City as shown on Alameda County’s official tax rolls, not on the property’s market value. Property owners should consult their own property tax bills to determine their property’s assessed value and any applicable tax exemptions. Attention of all voters is directed to the fact that the foregoing information is based upon projections and estimates only, which amounts are not maximum amounts or durations and are not binding upon the City. The actual debt service amounts, tax rates and the years in which they will apply may vary from those presently estimated, due to variations from these estimates in the rating for the bonds, the timing of bond sales, the amount of bonds sold and market interest rates at the time of each sale, and actual assessed valuations over the term of repayment of the bonds. The dates of sale and the amount of bonds sold at any given time will be determined by the City based on need for funds and other factors. The actual interest rates at which the bonds will be sold will depend on the bond market at the time of each sale. Actual future assessed valuation will depend upon the amount and value of taxable property within the City as determined by the Alameda County assessor in the annual assessment and the equalization process.

s ROSS MCCARTHY/ 
Finance Director, City of Alameda

strong: Vote Yes on L: a Safer Island for All Alamedans

text:
Flooded streets. Rising seas. Looming earthquakes. That’s the new reality for Alameda. The time to act is now. We all chose Alameda for its unique quality of life, but that quality of life depends on infrastructure that’s disaster ready.
As an island community, we’re on the front lines of sea-level rise. Severe storms and king tides aren’t rare — they’re routine. It’s no longer a question of if our streets, homes, and businesses will flood, it’s when.
Fire stations, storm sewers, and other critical infrastructure are decades old and don’t meet current earthquake safety standards. With an over 70% chance of a major earthquake in the coming decades, that’s not a risk we can afford to take. To make matters worse, the Federal Government has cut more than $50 million in grant funding for flooding and disaster preparedness just as the need is greatest. With so much uncertainty at the national level, we need a local solution to protect our island.
That’s why we need Measure L.
Prevent flooding in the Tubes and on City streets
Protect public safety during natural disasters
Repair potholes
Keep pollution out of the Bay
Maintain rapid response to fires, crashes, and medical emergencies
All funds stay local in Alameda — nothing can be taken by the State or Federal government
Independent citizens’ oversight and annual audits ensure every penny is spent as promised
By law, Measure L can’t fund salaries or pensions

A detailed project list outlines the use of all funds It’s on us to protect the strong, resilient island that makes Alameda worth calling home — for our neighbors, our property values, and the next generation of Alamedans. Please join us in voting Yes on L.
